implementation_notes: The data-shaped default: a @dataclass(frozen=True) descriptor holds the shared values (and, if needed, a callable slot for behaviour), a plain class holds per-instance state plus a reference to its descriptor, and a dict built from JSON or a config file is the registry. Frozen dataclasses make the immutability the pattern requires the default and give equality/repr for free, while dataclasses.replace() derives a tuned descriptor without mutating the shared one. Dataclasses exist since 3.7, so the floor is low; instances delegate explicitly (self.breed.attack) because no attribute magic is needed. Choose this over the runtime-class variant when types are pure data and testability matters - fixtures are just descriptor objects.
pitfalls: Sharing one mutable descriptor (a plain list of abilities, a dict of stats) between instances lets one instance's edit retune every sibling; freeze the descriptor and copy mutable members.
@dataclass(frozen=True) blocks attribute assignment but not mutation of objects the fields reference, and object.__setattr__ still bypasses it - treat frozen as a discipline, not a guarantee.
A class attribute used as the default descriptor is shared by every instance of that class; pass the breed into __init__ (or use field(default_factory=...)) instead.

variants.name: Types as real classes created at runtime
variants.idiom_name: type()/types.new_class built from data (+ metaclass registry)
variants.implementation_notes: Python can literally do what the paper describes - create new classes at runtime - so this variant builds each type definition into a real class: types.new_class(name, bases, exec_body=...) or a three-argument type() call over a namespace generated from the type data, with methods installed as functions (closures over the data, or a metaclass that reads the type table). Instances are then ordinary instances of those classes, per-type behaviour is real method dispatch, and isinstance/issubclass identity works, which is the reason to prefer this variant. It is the classic paper shape (TypeClass + Class, dynamic type creation, independent subclassing); prefer the descriptor variant when only data varies.
pitfalls: Classes created with type() are ordinary global state: they cannot be garbage collected while referenced by the registry, and re-registering the same id silently replaces the class, splitting isinstance identity between old and new instances.
Closures over spec keep the whole source dict alive for the lifetime of the class - relevant for large datasets - and make the generated methods invisible to debuggers and profilers.
Mixing this variant with dataclass/attrs descriptors for the same conceptual type breaks isinstance checks; pick one realization per type family, not per data file.
